name.text: 01 Question: Phonological Drift vs Substantive Variant

questiontext.text: <p>What is the essential philological difference between an orthographic variant and a substantive textual variant?</p>

answer.text: <p>Orthographic variants represent superficial phonetic or spelling differences that do not alter lexical identity or grammatical meaning, whereas substantive variants involve different words, omissions, additions, or major grammatical shifts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Orthographic variation reflects phonetic spelling or scribal habit without altering the semantic or lexical identity of the text.</p>

answer.text: <p>Orthographic variants only occur in printed editions, whereas substantive variants are restricted to handwritten manuscripts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Orthographic variation is ubiquitous across handwritten manuscript traditions.</p>

answer.text: <p>Orthographic variants must always be corrected silently without recording the manuscript's original spelling.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Scholarly digital editions preserve the manuscript witness in <orig> or diplomatic layers.</p>

answer.text: <p>Substantive variants are caused exclusively by physical damage to the parchment, whereas orthographic variants are caused by ink bleeding.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Substantive variants involve intentional or accidental linguistic changes by scribes, not merely physical parchment lacunae.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>In TEI P5 XML, how should an editor encode a manuscript word that exhibits historical spelling variation alongside a modern normalized form?</p>

answer.text: <p><choice><orig>diplomatic_form</orig><reg>normalized_form</reg></choice></p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. The <choice> element groups alternative encodings, with <orig> preserving the diplomatic manuscript witness and <reg> providing the regularized editorial form.</p>

answer.text: <p><subst><del>diplomatic_form</del><add>normalized_form</add></subst></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <subst> with <del> and <add> is reserved for physical scribal alterations on the manuscript page itself, not editorial regularization.</p>

answer.text: <p><abbr>diplomatic_form<expan>normalized_form</expan></abbr></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <abbr> and <expan> are used specifically for expanding scribal abbreviations, not for general orthographic regularization.</p>

answer.text: <p><choice><sic>diplomatic_form</sic><corr>normalized_form</corr></choice></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <sic> and <corr> indicate an overt scribal error, whereas orthographic variation is a recognized historical spelling rather than an error.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>What historical linguistic phenomenon is termed 'iotacism' in premodern and Hellenistic/Byzantine Greek manuscripts?</p>

answer.text: <p>The phonological convergence of several distinct vowels and diphthongs (such as ι, η, υ, ει, οι, υι) to the single vowel sound /i/, causing scribes to spell words phonetically.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Iotacism describes the phonetic merger of multiple front vowels and diphthongs into /i/, leading to widespread scribal interchange in spelling.</p>

answer.text: <p>The scribal practice of dropping the initial letter iota at the beginning of poetic verses.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Iotacism refers to vowel pronunciation convergence, not the omission of verse-initial letters.</p>

answer.text: <p>The systematic insertion of iota subscripts beneath capital uncial letters in ninth-century book hands.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. That relates to adscript/subscript history, not the phonetic phenomenon of iotacism.</p>

answer.text: <p>A machine learning classification error where a vision model mistakes the letter iota for a vertical stroke delimiter.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Iotacism is a well-known historical phonological development in the Greek language.</p>

name.text: 04 Question: Early Modern English Orthographic Fluidity

questiontext.text: <p>Which of the following describes a standard orthographic convention in early modern English handwritten documents?</p>

answer.text: <p>Positional interchange of 'u' and 'v' (where 'v' often appeared initially and 'u' medially) and 'i' and 'j', regardless of vowel or consonant status.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. In pre-17th-century English writing, 'v' was standard initially (e.g. 'vnder') and 'u' medially (e.g. 'haue').</p>

answer.text: <p>Strict adherence to 18th-century Samuel Johnson dictionary spellings across all personal letters.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Standardized dictionary orthography was not established until centuries later.</p>

answer.text: <p>Mandatory hyphenation between every syllable in legal petitions.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Premodern legal scribes did not systematically hyphenate syllables.</p>

answer.text: <p>The universal omission of all terminal silent '-e' letters in 16th-century court hands.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Terminal '-e' was exceptionally common and fluid in early modern orthography.</p>

name.text: 05 Question: Pitfalls of Global Regex Normalization

questiontext.text: <p>Why is executing a naive global string replacement like `s/vn/un/g` in a normalization script hazardous in historical texts?</p>

answer.text: <p>Without word-boundary delimiters (`\b`), it will corrupt unrelated words containing that character sequence in both source and target contexts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Regex replacement without word boundaries (`\b`) will unintentionally modify substrings inside larger words.</p>

answer.text: <p>Python's `re` module cannot process text encodings other than 7-bit ASCII.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Python 3's `re` module natively supports full Unicode strings.</p>

answer.text: <p>XML parsers treat regular expressions as dangerous security exploits and refuse to open the document.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. XML parsers process static text content and do not evaluate external regex scripts.</p>

answer.text: <p>Global regex substitution permanently deletes the git commit history of the repository.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Regex scripts only alter the working directory files until committed.</p>

name.text: 06 Question: AI Hypercorrection and Dialectal Erasure

questiontext.text: <p>What is the danger of using an unconstrained commercial LLM to 'clean up the spelling' of a premodern manuscript transcription?</p>

answer.text: <p>The model tends to 'hypercorrect' authentic regional dialectal features and historical phonological spellings, erasing crucial linguistic and provenance evidence.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. LLMs trained on modern standardized text tend to aggressively modernize idiosyncratic scribal spellings, destroying historical dialect data.</p>

answer.text: <p>The LLM will automatically convert the text into binary machine code.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. LLMs output natural language text, not machine code.</p>

answer.text: <p>The LLM will delete all vowels from the document due to tokenization compression.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Tokenization preserves standard characters and words.</p>

answer.text: <p>The model will notify copyright authorities that the historical text is unauthorized.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Historical manuscript texts are public domain and do not trigger copyright notifications.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Why do scholarly digital editions prioritize storing both diplomatic and regularized forms rather than replacing the text outright?</p>

answer.text: <p>To ensure verifiable reproducibility, allowing readers and computational tools to toggle between the physical artifact's actual writing and a normalized reading view.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Digital editions maintain epistemological integrity by keeping the exact manuscript witness alongside interpretive editorial normalizations.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because TEI schemas throw a fatal error whenever an XML document contains fewer than two distinct spellings per sentence.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. TEI schemas enforce structural hierarchy and attributes, not an arbitrary word count rule.</p>

answer.text: <p>To double the file size in order to meet grant funding storage quotas.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Academic editions prioritize scholarly rigor and verifiability, not artificial file inflation.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because web browsers cannot render historical alphabets unless accompanied by modern translations.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Web browsers render historical Unicode characters perfectly well with proper font support.</p>

name.text: 08 Question: Normalization as a Collation Baseline

questiontext.text: <p>What vital role does orthographic normalization play prior to automated computer-assisted collation across multiple witnesses?</p>

answer.text: <p>It prevents trivial spelling variations from generating thousands of false-positive variant readings, allowing collators to focus on substantive textual divergences.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Normalization creates a clean linguistic baseline so automated collation algorithms highlight substantive variants rather than orthographic noise.</p>

answer.text: <p>It reorders the manuscript witnesses according to their physical parchment thickness.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Collation compares textual sequences, not physical leaf thickness.</p>

answer.text: <p>It eliminates the need for human editors to ever consult the original manuscripts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. High-resolution facsimiles and physical codices must always be consulted to verify substantive cruxes.</p>

answer.text: <p>It forces all historical manuscripts into exact chronological order based on vowel counts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Normalization aligns spelling, not chronological dating.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Which Python regular expression pattern correctly identifies the archaic initial 'v' representing a vowel (e.g. 'vnder', 'vnto') at the start of a word while preserving trailing letters?</p>

answer.text: <p>\b[vV]([a-z]+)\b</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. The pattern uses word boundaries `\b` and captures subsequent letters in group 1, allowing safe replacement with `u\1` or `U\1`.</p>

answer.text: <p>.*v.*</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. `.*v.*` matches any line containing the letter 'v' anywhere in the line.</p>

answer.text: <p>[vV]</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. A bare character set without word boundaries matches every 'v' inside any word (e.g. 'every', 'have').</p>

answer.text: <p>^v$</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. `^v$` only matches a line containing a single isolated letter 'v'.</p>

name.text: 10 Question: Quality Auditing of Normalization Passes

questiontext.text: <p>In the three-step comparative cycle (manual -> deterministic -> AI-assisted), how does an editor verify the reliability of an automated normalization pipeline?</p>

answer.text: <p>By calculating precision, recall, and error rate of the automated passes against the hand-encoded manual ground-truth sample.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Quantitative evaluation against a curated manual ground truth reveals both missed normalizations (false negatives) and over-regularizations (false positives).</p>

answer.text: <p>By assuming that if the script completes without an exception, 100% of the words were normalized correctly.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. A script can run to completion while corrupting data or missing edge cases.</p>

answer.text: <p>By relying solely on the LLM's self-generated claim that its output is perfectly accurate.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Generative AI models cannot objectively audit their own hallucination rates.</p>

answer.text: <p>By discarding all original files and keeping only the final AI output.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. That violates basic digital scholarship and data preservation principles.</p>
